--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.network_proximity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute network proximity between two sets of nodes. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.network_proximity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute network proximity between two sets of nodes. title: >- [Graph.network_proximity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Compute network proximity between two sets of nodes. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute network proximity between two sets of nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L52398-L52561){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.network_proximity( set_a, set_b, method="closest", ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Network proximity](../assets/graphs/network-proximity.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The eight-gene network with gene set A = G1, G2 in teal and set B = G6, G8 in violet. The closest pair is G2 and G6, three steps apart through the bridge G4 to G5, drawn in the accent color. The card reports that all 4 cross-set pairs are reachable and the closest-pair proximity is 3." width="100%"} Measures how close two groups of nodes are in the network using shortest-path distances. Useful for drug-target vs. disease-gene proximity analysis and network-based drug repurposing. The method computes the shortest-path distance from every node in `set_a=` to every node in `set_b=` and then summarizes those distances according to `method=`. A node that appears in both sets is at distance `0` from itself. Pairs with no connecting path are left out of the summary, and the `reachable_pairs` and `total_pairs` values in the result tell you how many pairs that affected. Typical uses include: - drug-disease proximity: how close a drug's targets sit to a disease's genes - comparing two disease modules to see whether they share a network neighborhood - testing whether a gene set is unusually close to a set of known hits (compare the result against random sets of the same size) Distances follow the graph's structure: in directed graphs paths must follow edge direction (so the result can depend on which set is `set_a=`), and in weighted graphs edge weights are summed as path lengths. Each node in `set_a=` triggers one single-source shortest-path search, so cost grows with the size of `set_a=` times the size of the graph. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [set_a]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The first set of nodes, as a list of node IDs or string labels. Must be non-empty and every node must be in the graph. In directed graphs, paths are measured from these nodes. [set_b]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The second set of nodes, as a list of node IDs or string labels. Must be non-empty and every node must be in the graph. It may share nodes with `set_a=`. [method]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["closest"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Proximity measure to use (the default is `"closest"`): - `"closest"`: minimum shortest-path distance across all (a, b) pairs. - `"shortest"`: average shortest-path distance across all reachable pairs. - `"kernel"`: average of `exp(-d)` over all reachable pairs (diffusion kernel similarity). Unlike the two above, larger values mean the sets are closer. - `"separation"`: network separation `d_AB - (d_AA + d_BB) / 2` (after Menche et al., *Science* 2015), where `d_AB` is the mean distance between the sets and `d_AA`, `d_BB` are the mean pairwise distances within each set (`0` for a single-node set). Negative values indicate overlapping neighborhoods. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : For `"closest"`, `"shortest"`, `"kernel"`: a dictionary with keys `proximity`, `reachable_pairs`, `total_pairs` (all floats). If no pair is reachable, `proximity` is `inf` for `"closest"` and `"shortest"` and `0.0` for `"kernel"`. For `"separation"`: a dictionary with keys `separation`, `d_ab`, `d_aa`, `d_bb`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If either set is empty, if a node is not in the graph, or if `method=` is not one of the four supported values. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~shortest_path_length`) : The distance between two nodes. [](`~random_walk_with_restart`) : Score nodes by their closeness to a set of seeds. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a five-node path, the closest pair between `{A, B}` and `{D, E}` is `B` and `D`, two steps apart. The sets are further apart (`d_ab` of `3.0`) than the members of each are from each other (`1.0`), so their separation is positive: ::: {#8e7a2379 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec path = ec.Graph.from_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E")]) ( path.network_proximity(["A", "B"], ["D", "E"]), path.network_proximity(["A", "B"], ["D", "E"], method="separation"), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ({'proximity': 2.0, 'reachable_pairs': 4.0, 'total_pairs': 4.0}, {'separation': 2.0, 'd_ab': 3.0, 'd_aa': 1.0, 'd_bb': 1.0}) ``` ::: ::: ### How close a drug is to a disease `proteins()` is a small protein interaction network with five known disease genes and the targets of two drugs. Drug A binds REP6 and CYC3, and Drug B binds SIG4 and ENZ2: ::: {#846ccaf3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl proteins = ec.proteins() disease = ["REP1", "REP2", "REP5", "CYC2", "TRN3"] targets = { drug: proteins.get_node_df().filter(pl.col("drug_target") == drug)["label"].to_list() for drug in ["Drug A", "Drug B"] } targets ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'Drug A': ['REP6', 'CYC3'], 'Drug B': ['SIG4', 'ENZ2']} ``` ::: ::: Each of Drug A's targets binds a disease gene, while Drug B's are three steps from the nearest one. By every measure Drug A is the closer, and its separation is negative: its targets sit inside the neighborhood of the disease genes: ::: {#88febd17 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.DataFrame( { "method": ["closest", "shortest", "kernel"], **{ drug: [ proteins.network_proximity(t, disease, method=m)["proximity"] for m in ["closest", "shortest", "kernel"] ] for drug, t in targets.items() }, } ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
